idiom_name: ASP.NET Core session middleware (AddSession / UseSession) over IDistributedCache
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core ships the pattern as middleware: register a cache (AddDistributedMemoryCache for one instance, Redis/SQL Server/Azure Cache for a farm), call AddSession and UseSession in the right pipeline position, and HttpContext.Session exposes ISession with Get/Set/Remove plus the GetString/SetString/GetInt32 helpers; the framework sets the .AspNetCore.Session cookie, which by default is HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax and carries only the session id. The payload lives in whatever IDistributedCache was registered, which is the documented way to avoid sticky sessions in a server farm, and SessionOptions.IdleTimeout (20 minutes by default) is the store-side expiry. Two documented details shape the realization: the default provider loads the record synchronously unless LoadAsync is called first, and the session is coherent and non-locking, so concurrent requests resolve as last-writer-wins.
pitfalls: The in-memory cache provider stores records in the node's own memory: behind a load balancer it needs sticky sessions (which the docs call worse for scalability) or a distributed cache, and records die with the process.

Empty sessions are not retained - a session with no values gives each request a fresh id - and the framework cannot tell the app that the browser was closed, so server-side expiry is the only reliable lifetime control.
Session state and SignalR/Blazor Server do not mix: a hub may execute outside an HTTP context, so per-connection state belongs in hub Items instead.
